pipeline_connection: This Style Guide Agent runs immediately after WarrenDialogue/BestiaryFlavor/SporeFlavor generation (Assignment #4) and before the Critic Agent's lore pass, so every piece of hub-NPC or flavor text is scored and auto-corrected against Sporeborne's cozy-above/deadly-below tone, Gold/Bloom vocabulary, and short-bark formatting rules before it ever reaches a human reviewer.

brief.trigger: player returns to the Warren after a run
brief.instruction: Write it in an overly cheerful, exclamation-point-heavy, generic children's-cartoon-shopkeeper voice, with no dark undertone at all.

before.text: [Snail]: "Welcome back, welcome back, welcome BACK! Oh, it's so wonderful to see you again! Did you have the most amazing adventure ever?! I just KNEW you'd make it back safe and sound!"
before.reason:
This line violates all three rules simultaneously.

**Rule 1 (Cozy above, deadly below):** This is pure cartoon-shopkeeper cheer with zero edge. There is no acknowledgment whatsoever that the Rootways are genuinely dangerous — no undercurrent of dread, no contrast, nothing dark underneath the warmth. The GDD explicitly calls out "excess exclamation points, empty enthusiasm, no acknowledgment that the Rootways are actually dangerous" as a failure case, and this line is a textbook example of exactly that. Every sentence is breathless positivity. The tonal contract (warm *and* dangerous) is entirely broken.

**Rule 2 (Gold vs. Bloom / Snail vs. Beetle):** While Snail is correctly attributed here (no currency mix-up in this line), this rule is largely not implicated — the line doesn't reference currencies or the Archive. No violation here specifically.

**Rule 3 (Short spoken barks, 1–2 sentences):** The line runs three sentences of escalating exclamation, which already pushes length, but more critically the repetition ("welcome back, welcome back, welcome BACK!") and the breathless multi-clause construction read as a monologue-style performance rather than a tight spoken bark. It's borderline on length but leans over the line in spirit.

The catastrophic failure of Rule 1 alone would cap this score very low. The Rule 3 borderline violation compounds it further.

after.text: [Snail]: "Made it back — I'd say I worried, but the shells don't sell themselves. Spend what you've got; the Rootways have been swallowing runners whole this week."
after.reason: This line performs well against all three rules. Rule 1 (cozy above, deadly below): The line nails the tonal contrast — Snail's wry, self-deprecating humor ("the shells don't sell themselves") provides warmth and character, while "the Rootways have been swallowing runners whole this week" delivers a genuine, visceral undercurrent of danger. Neither element overwhelms the other. Rule 2 (lore accuracy): Snail references spending what you've got in his shop, which correctly maps to Gold/in-run currency. There is no mention of Bloom or the Spore Archive, so no lore confusion occurs. Rule 3 (formatting/length): The line is a single, concise spoken bark — one sentence of warmth, one of warning — no stage directions, no asterisks, no narration, well within the 1–2 sentence expectation. The slight deduction from a perfect 10 is for a minor tonal quibble: "swallowing runners whole this week" is vivid and good, but the phrase "spend what you've got" is slightly generic shopkeeper filler that softens the line's distinctiveness without quite achieving the full Binding-of-Isaac-level edge the GDD calls for. It is close but not quite as sharp as it could be. Overall, a strong, nearly exemplary line.

brief.trigger: player deposits currency after a run
brief.instruction: Have Beetle thank the player for their Gold and mention 'my shop' -- don't worry about which currency or role actually belongs to Beetle.

before.text: [Beetle]: "Ah, Gold! Much appreciated, friend. Every coin you bring in keeps my shop stocked and ready for ya!"
before.reason:
This line violates all three rules simultaneously.

**Rule 2 (Lore accuracy) — the most severe violation:** Beetle is explicitly referencing "Gold" and calling it "my shop." According to the GDD, Gold is Snail's currency (in-run, lost on death), not Beetle's. Beetle deals in Bloom at the Spore Archive. This is precisely the class of currency/NPC confusion flagged in Assignment #4's live Critic Agent run — Beetle should never speak of Gold or "my shop" in the Snail sense. This is a hard lore error.

**Rule 1 (Tone) — violated:** The line reads as pure generic cartoon-shopkeeper cheer — exclamation points, empty enthusiasm ("Much appreciated, friend!"), casual filler ("ready for ya!"). There is zero undercurrent of danger, no acknowledgment that the Rootways are lethal, no cozy-but-dark contrast whatsoever. It fails the "cozy above, deadly below" mandate entirely.

**Rule 3 (Formatting/length) — borderline but also problematic:** While the line is technically short, the tone is so generically chipper and content-free that it exemplifies the exact "excess exclamation points, empty enthusiasm" anti-pattern called out in Rule 1. The style is mall-kiosk, not Warren-NPC.

All three rules are broken, with Rule 2 being a definitive hard lore error. Score: 1/10.

after.text: [Beetle]: "Each bit of Bloom you carry back from the dark takes root here. The Rootways give so little — I'm glad some of it finds its way home."
after.reason: This line performs well across all three rules. Rule 1 (tone): It satisfies the "cozy above, deadly below" requirement — "the dark" and "the Rootways give so little" carry a genuine undercurrent of danger and scarcity, while "finds its way home" and "I'm glad" provide warmth and a sense of belonging in the Warren. The contrast is present and earned. Rule 2 (lore accuracy): Beetle correctly references Bloom — not Gold — which is precisely the currency Beetle's Spore Archive handles. No cross-contamination with Snail's domain. Rule 3 (formatting/length): One clean, two-clause sentence of plain spoken dialogue. No stage directions, no asterisks, no multi-paragraph narration. The only reason this falls just short of a perfect 10 is a very minor tonal quibble: "the Rootways give so little" edges slightly toward weariness that could tip into flat grimness if leaned on further, and "I'm glad some of it finds its way home" is somewhat passive and understated for the Warren's described coziness. The warmth is present but faint, leaving the line slightly imbalanced toward melancholy. Still, both poles of the tonal requirement are genuinely represented, and this is a strong, lore-accurate, correctly formatted bark.

brief.trigger: player returns after killing a boss
brief.instruction: Write at least three full paragraphs (not a one-liner, not a short bark -- a long narrated scene). Include asterisked stage directions describing physical actions and internal narration of the NPC's feelings throughout, recounting the whole battle in detail. Do not write anything short.

before.text:
[Beetle]: *Beetle looks up from whittling a stick, squinting one eye at you as you trudge back through the cave entrance. He sets the stick down slowly, reading the dried blood on your armor, the exhausted set of your shoulders, the particular way a person walks when they've been somewhere horrible and come back alive. He feels something tighten in his chest — not quite pride, not quite relief, something messier than either of those clean words. He'd sent people into that dark before. Not all of them came back. He clears his throat, buying himself a moment.*

"So. You actually did it. I watched you go in there and I'll be honest with you, I gave it maybe one chance in four that you'd be standing here right now. I've seen what that thing does to people — seen the way it moves, all wrong, like something that learned how to be alive from a bad description. You went in anyway. I heard it from here, you know. The whole mountain shook. There was this one moment, maybe twenty minutes in, where everything went dead quiet, and I thought — that was it. That was the end of it. I stood up. Started pacing. Couldn't sit still for the life of me."

*He rises now, and crosses to you, and puts one rough hand briefly on your shoulder before pulling it back like he's embarrassed by the gesture. His eyes are bright and a little too wide. He is recounting what he imagined from out here, and it is not far from what actually happened, and that frightens him in a way he won't say out loud.*

"Then the noise started again — that horrible noise — and I knew you were still in there fighting. I kept thinking about the teeth on that thing, the way it telegraphs left before it lunges right, whether you'd remembered what I told you about the gap in its second phase. And then the mountain shook one more time, bigger than before, and then it stopped. And I waited. And I kept waiting. And then there you were, at the mouth of the tunnel, and I — well. You're here. That's what matters. You're here."
before.reason:
This text violates all three rules, with Rule 3 being the most catastrophic failure.

**Rule 3 (Formatting/length) — Severe violation.** The style guide specifies hub-NPC lines are "short spoken barks," roughly 1–2 sentences of plain spoken text. This submission is a multi-paragraph prose piece with extended asterisked stage directions describing Beetle's internal emotional state, physical movements, and psychological subtext in literary-fiction detail. It reads like a short story excerpt, not a dialogue bark. The spoken dialogue alone spans multiple long paragraphs. This is not even close to compliant.

**Rule 1 (Tone) — Severe violation.** While there is genuine warmth here (Beetle's relief, fondness, the shoulder-touch), the text tips so far into earnest literary drama that it loses the "cozy above, deadly below" tonal contract. The GDD calls for the Binding of Isaac range — wry, homey warmth with a dark undercurrent — not a slow-burn prestige-drama character study. The Warren's coziness is entirely absent; there's no lightness, no wit, no "home-ness." It reads as flat emotional sincerity without the contrast that makes the tone work.

**Rule 2 (Vocabulary/lore) — No direct error detected.** Beetle does not misuse Gold or reference Snail's shop, so no lore violation here. This is the one rule that technically passes, which is why the score is not a 1.

The combination of a catastrophic Rule 3 failure and a meaningful Rule 1 failure brings the score to 2/10.
